date_label: Known only from a letter of 2 September 1900, by which time he had returned to Naples; when and where Wilde knew him is not stated
summary: Wilde called him one of 'my dear Neapolitans' and said he missed him after the group went home. The whole of the record is one sentence in a letter to his publisher, in which he weighs a waiter in Paris against him and finds the waiter no consolation.

sources.quote: Is there any chance of your being in Paris? My dear Neapolitans have returned to Naples and I miss that brown faun with his deep woodland eyes and his sensuous grace of limb. A slim brown Egyptian, rather like a handsome bamboo walking-stick, occasionally serves me drinks at the Cafe d'Egypte, but he does not console me for the loss of the wanton sylvan boy of Italy.
sources.context: Wilde to Leonard Smithers, [Postmark 2 September 1900], Paris - three months before his death. The same sentence introduces the Cafe d'Egypte waiter, who has his own entry; the two are different men, and the sentence turns on the contrast between them.
sources.supports: The association and its ending, in Wilde's own words, and the terms he describes him in.
sources.provenance: PDF p. 1242. 'Cafe d'Egypte' carries an acute accent in the printed text; accents normalised here. The letter is incomplete and descends from a printed memoir and a saleroom catalogue rather than a manuscript - see the editors' footnote 1 on the same page.
